passage: After school in the village of Kalwan, Mahima asked Nitin to explain photosynthesis before Monday's test. Nitin had topped science every year. He leaned on the school wall and rattled it off. "Easy. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which drives the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Light reaction, dark reaction. Done." Mahima blinked. "What's chlorophyll?" "The green pigment, obviously." "What's a pigment?" Nitin sighed loudly. "Mahima, we did this in Class 7." She went quiet and looked at her slippers. Nitin walked home thinking she was just slow. At dinner his younger cousin asked him what a pigment was. Nitin started to answer, then stopped. He remembered not knowing that word himself, once. He had forgotten what it was like.

qa.q: What did Mahima ask Nitin to explain?
qa.a: Photosynthesis.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when Mahima kept asking questions?
qa.a: He felt impatient and irritated, sighing loudly, because the topic felt so easy to him that he thought she was slow.

qa.q: What could Nitin do differently when he explains it again?
qa.a: Use plain words and small steps, like explaining that chlorophyll is the green colour in leaves that catches sunlight, and check what Mahima already knows.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when Nitin said "we did this in Class 7"?
qa.a: Mahima felt embarrassed and small, going quiet and looking at her slippers.

grounding: Shows a teenager who knows a topic well explaining it too fast with jargon and thinking the listener is slow.

passage: In the computer lab of their Johannesburg school, Lindiwe was helping Valentina with loops for the coding assignment. Lindiwe had been coding since she was eleven. "It's simple," she said, typing fast. "You initialise the iterator, set the condition, increment, and the body executes until the condition's false. Then you break out. See?" Valentina stared at the screen. "What's an iterator?" "The counter variable." "What's a variable?" Lindiwe laughed, not kindly. "Seriously? It's week six." Valentina's face went red. She closed her notebook. "Never mind. I'll figure it out." Lindiwe shrugged and went back to her own work, thinking Valentina just wasn't trying. Later, the teacher explained loops to the class using a skipping rope: "Jump ten times, count each jump, stop at ten." Valentina's hand went up first with the right answer.

qa.q: What did the teacher use to explain loops to the class?
qa.a: A skipping rope.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe laugh at Valentina's question?
qa.a: Lindiwe felt impatient and a little superior, because coding felt so obvious to her that she couldn't imagine not knowing what a variable is.

qa.q: What does the teacher's skipping-rope example suggest Lindiwe could try?
qa.a: Explaining with a simple, everyday example and plain words instead of jargon, starting from what the listener already knows.

qa.q: How did Valentina feel when Lindiwe laughed?
qa.a: Valentina felt embarrassed and hurt, her face going red, and she gave up asking.

grounding: Shows a teenager who knows coding well explaining too fast with jargon and assuming her classmate is slow.

passage: In the school library, two days before the maths exam, Vasudha agreed to help Nikita with trigonometry. Vasudha had finished the whole syllabus in October. "So, sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cos is adjacent over hypotenuse, tan is opposite over adjacent. Use the identity, substitute, and simplify. That's all," she said in one breath. Nikita looked at the triangle. "Which side is opposite?" "Opposite the angle. Obviously." "Which angle?" Vasudha rolled her eyes. "The one in the question!" The librarian looked up. Nikita whispered, "Sorry, I'm just dumb at this." Vasudha thought, maybe she is. Then the librarian came over, drew a triangle, and put a small smiley face at one corner. "Stand here, at the smiley. The side across from you is opposite. The one next to you is adjacent." Nikita nodded slowly. Vasudha felt a little ashamed.

qa.q: When had Vasudha finished the whole syllabus?
qa.a: In October.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling by the end of the scene?
qa.a: She felt a little ashamed, seeing that Nikita needed a starting point she had forgotten, not that Nikita was dumb.

qa.q: What did the librarian do that worked?
qa.a: The librarian drew a triangle with a smiley face at one corner, giving Nikita a simple place to stand before naming the sides.

qa.q: How did Nikita see herself after Vasudha's quick explanation?
qa.a: Nikita felt dumb and embarrassed, apologising for not understanding.

grounding: Shows a teenager who knows trigonometry well explaining too fast and thinking her classmate is slow, until someone explains from the beginning.

passage: At the gram panchayat hall in Sangole, Yash, a third-year agriculture student, stood up to present his project on soil health to fifty farmers. He had rehearsed it perfectly for his professors. "Namaskar. So, the soil test shows low NPK and poor CEC, so we recommend IPM plus site-specific nutrient management, with FYM and bio-fertilisers per the SHC." He looked up. Blank faces. Someone's phone rang. An old farmer at the back said, "Beta, what is NPK?" Yash blinked. Everyone in his college knew NPK. He tried again, faster. Two farmers left for tea. Lakshmi, a farmer who ran the women's group, raised her hand. "Tell us what to put in the field, in our words." Yash stood there, face hot. He had lost the room within a minute and hadn't even noticed.

qa.q: How many farmers did Yash present to?
qa.a: Fifty farmers.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when the old farmer asked what NPK was?
qa.a: He felt surprised and flustered, because everyone in his college knew NPK and he hadn't thought the farmers might not.

qa.q: What could Yash do to reach the farmers?
qa.a: Use their words and examples, explaining what to put in the field without acronyms, as Lakshmi asked.

qa.q: How did the farmers experience the start of Yash's talk?
qa.a: They felt lost and bored, with blank faces, a phone ringing and two leaving for tea.

grounding: Shows a student presenter using acronyms the audience doesn't know and losing them in the first minute.

passage: In the seminar room at the university in Manchester, Chidi stood up to present his research to the first-year students. It was his favourite topic. "Right, so our RCT used a DiD approach with FE at the district level, and we clustered SEs to handle ICC. The ATE was significant." He clicked to the next slide. Valentina, in the front row, had stopped writing after the second word. Around her, people were checking their phones. Chidi didn't notice. He was already on the next slide. At the end, the tutor asked if anyone had questions. Silence. Afterwards, Valentina told him, kindly, "It sounded brilliant. I just didn't understand one word after 'Right, so.'" Chidi looked at his slides. Every term had felt as normal as breathing. He had forgotten that he had once needed them explained too.

qa.q: When did Valentina stop writing?
qa.a: After the second word.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling when Valentina spoke to him afterwards?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a bit embarrassed, seeing that terms that felt normal to him meant nothing to his audience.

qa.q: What could Chidi change for his next presentation?
qa.a: Explain each term in plain words or skip acronyms, and check the audience is with him before moving on.

qa.q: What was the seminar like for Valentina?
qa.a: Valentina was lost almost from the start and kept her kindness while admitting she didn't understand.

grounding: Shows a student presenter using jargon and acronyms the audience doesn't know, losing them in the first minute without noticing.

passage: The college's orientation week in Pune had senior students giving short talks to freshers. Sumit, a final-year engineering student, was proud of his talk on the college's robotics club. He began: "So we use ROS on a Raspberry-based SBC with PID control and SLAM for navigation..." He paused for a laugh that didn't come. The freshers stared at him. One girl in the front row, Manjula, frowned and wrote "ROS?" in her notebook, then crossed it out. Sumit kept going, a little faster. By the third slide, half the hall was whispering. At the end, only two people signed up for the club. Sumit complained to his friend that freshers these days weren't curious. His friend asked, "Did you explain what SLAM means?" Sumit opened his mouth. Then closed it. He had thought everyone knew.

qa.q: How many people signed up for the club at the end?
qa.a: Only two people signed up for the club.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling after the talk, and how did it change?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and blamed the freshers, then uneasy when his friend asked if he had explained SLAM.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Sumit assumed freshers knew the acronyms; he could start with what the robot does, in plain words, before any technical terms.

qa.q: What was the talk like for Manjula?
qa.a: Manjula felt lost and gave up trying to note the terms, crossing out her question in the notebook.

grounding: Shows a student presenter using acronyms that freshers don't know and losing the room in the first minute.

passage:
Field note, water project, Champhai, 3 April.
Sangeeta, our new filtration engineer, was to explain the new village water filter at the community hall tomorrow. Her first draft was full of words like "turbidity" and "microbial load." Tonight, without being asked, she practised it on the cook at our guest house, who had never studied science. When the cook looked lost, Sangeeta stopped, laughed at herself, and started over: "The filter is like a very fine cloth. The sand catches the mud, the stones catch the bigger dirt, and the tiny living things get stuck in a slimy layer on top." Then she asked the cook to explain it back. The cook did, perfectly, with hand movements.
I've asked her to use the same version tomorrow.
Lalremsiami

qa.q: Who did Sangeeta practise her explanation on?
qa.a: The cook at our guest house, who had never studied science.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta laughing at herself suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed relaxed and good-humoured, amused rather than embarrassed to find her first draft too technical.

qa.q: Which part of Sangeeta's approach should others copy, and why?
qa.a: Testing on someone outside the field, using a plain example like a fine cloth, and asking the listener to explain it back, which checks real understanding.

qa.q: How might the cook have felt explaining it back?
qa.a: The cook probably felt proud and involved, able to explain a new idea with hand movements.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a skilled engineer testing her explanation on an outsider, using plain words and examples, and asking the listener to say it back.

passage:
Sunday.
Tried to explain cloud backup to Lakshmi Maasi today, because she keeps losing her photos. First attempt, I said "servers," "sync" and "encryption" in one breath. She nodded politely, which I know means she understood nothing.
So I started over. "Maasi, you know how you keep a copy of your ration card at Nani's house, in case yours gets lost? The cloud is like that. A copy of your photos kept safely in a big locked cupboard far away." She smiled. "So if my phone falls in the well, the photos are still at Nani's?" Exactly.
Then I asked her to explain it back to me. She did, with the ration card and all.
Note to self: I'm Devika, the engineer, and I forget that not everyone lives inside my words.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi Maasi keep losing?
qa.a: Her photos.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when Maasi nodded politely the first time?
qa.a: Devika felt a little uneasy, knowing the polite nod meant Maasi had understood nothing of the technical words.

qa.q: What did Devika do that made the explanation work?
qa.a: Devika used a familiar example, a copy of the ration card at Nani's house, and asked Maasi to explain it back.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi Maasi feel after the second explanation?
qa.a: Maasi seemed pleased and confident, smiling and putting the idea in her own words about the phone falling in the well.

grounding: A young engineer's diary shows testing an explanation on an outsider, switching to a plain example, and asking the listener to say it back.

passage: It was the last day of the Onam holidays, and rain was hammering the tin roof. Madhav had helped Amma make the flower carpet all morning. "Beautiful! Clever boy!" she said. Then he knocked over the water pot, and she said sharply, "Madhav, careful!" At bedtime, his older cousin Nitin asked, "How was your day?" Madhav's lip wobbled. "Amma shouted at me." "What else?" "Just the shouting." Nitin laughed. "She said 'clever boy' about ten times. I counted." Madhav thought. "She did?" "And the flowers?" Madhav looked at the carpet. "I made the yellow part," he whispered.

qa.q: What did Madhav knock over?
qa.a: The water pot.

qa.q: Why did Madhav only remember the shouting at bedtime?
qa.a: The one sharp word hurt so much that he felt sad and small, and it pushed out all the praise from the morning.

qa.q: How did Nitin help Madhav remember the good parts?
qa.a: He told Madhav that Amma said "clever boy" about ten times and pointed him to the flower carpet he made.

qa.a: Amma might feel sad and surprised, since she had praised him many times and only spoken sharply once.

passage: One cold winter morning in Lucknow, Vijay's playschool made paper lanterns for the Christmas fair. Miss praised Vijay three times: for his bright colours, for sharing glue, for helping Pranav fold his lantern. Then Vijay tore the paper by mistake, and Miss said, "Oh, Vijay, gently!" At home, his mother asked about school. "Miss was angry with me," Vijay said, hiding his face in her shawl. "Anything else?" "No." Pranav's mother laughed. "Pranav said Miss told Vijay he was the best helper." Vijay peeked out. "She did?" He showed his mother his lantern.

qa.q: How many times did Miss praise Vijay?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he hid his face in his mother's shawl?
qa.a: He felt sad and ashamed, as if Miss had only been angry, because the one sharp word stuck more than the praise.

qa.q: How did Pranav's mother's news help Vijay?
qa.a: It reminded him that Miss called him the best helper, so he remembered the good parts of his day.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel about telling his mother Vijay was the best helper?
qa.a: Pranav probably felt happy for his friend and proud to share good news.

grounding: Shows a young child remembering one sharp word from his teacher more than three bits of praise during a winter craft day.

passage: In the village school in Barshi, the Class 5 teacher returned the story notebooks with comments. passage: At the end of term at her school in Valencia, Hana's report card came home. Her teacher had written about her reading, kindness, painting and more: nine happy lines. Hana frowned. "But the bad one is true." "So are the nine," her father said. Hana read the report again, slowly this time. "She said my painting is brave," she said softly.

qa.a: She felt hurt and upset, sure the teacher thought she was annoying because of the one critical line.

qa.q: What helped Hana see the whole report?
qa.a: Santiago counting nine good lines and one bad, and her father saying the nine were true too, so she reread it slowly.

qa.q: How might Hana's father see the report?

passage: At the art club in the community centre in Mysore, Ira ma'am looked at each clay pot. She stopped at Chaitanya's. "Lovely shape. Nice smooth sides. Good idea with the handle. Great colours." passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10B, 16 August.
Neelam has seemed low since Monday. Today she told me why. At the debate practice, a boy muttered that her English "sounded like a village girl." She has thought about it every day since.
I asked what else people said at the practice. She shrugged. So I read her the feedback forms I had collected. The judges wrote that her argument was the strongest. Her teammates wrote "fearless" and "clear." Seven positive notes, one unkind mutter.
She said, "But the mutter felt real." I understand. Hurtful words stick harder. I have spoken to the boy separately about the remark. With Neelam, I suggested she keep the feedback forms and read them before the next debate. She took them home.

qa.q: How many positive notes were on the feedback forms?
qa.a: Seven positive notes, one unkind mutter.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling since Monday?
qa.a: She felt low and hurt, thinking every day about the one unkind remark about her English.

qa.q: What did the teacher do, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: The teacher read Neelam the positive feedback, spoke to the boy separately about the remark, and suggested she reread the forms before the next debate.

qa.q: How did Neelam's teammates see her at the practice?
qa.a: Her teammates saw her as fearless and clear, the opposite of what the unkind remark suggested.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager replaying one mocking comment for days while overlooking warm praise from judges and teammates.

passage: In the girls' hostel at the Delhi university, Chandrika had started checking the news app every hour. Floods in one state, a train accident in another, a scam, a heatwave warning. At night she lay in bed scrolling until two, her heart racing. "Everything is falling apart," she told her roommate Anjali at breakfast, tired and pale. "The world is getting worse and worse." Anjali asked, "What good news did you read this week?" Chandrika stared at her. "None." "Nothing? Not the new metro line, or the village schools that got solar lights, or your own cousin's result?" Chandrika hadn't looked. The warden, passing by, suggested she keep her phone outside the room at night and talk to the college counsellor if the worry didn't ease. That night Chandrika left her phone on the corridor charging shelf. She slept until seven.

qa.a: Until two.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling at breakfast?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exhausted, convinced the world was falling apart because she only read bad news.

qa.q: What helped Chandrika, and what could she keep doing?
qa.a: Anjali asking about good news and the warden's advice to keep the phone outside at night; she can limit scrolling and talk to the counsellor if the worry stays.

qa.a: Anjali sees both bad and good news, like the new metro line and solar lights, so the world doesn't look as dark to her.

passage:
Dear Sahil,
You asked why I've been so quiet lately. I think it's the news. Every night since March, I read everything bad: wars, floods, crime, layoffs. I go to sleep feeling like the whole world is burning and there's no point in anything. I'm tired all the time.
Yesterday I did an experiment my professor suggested. I counted the stories I read in one evening. Forty-two. Thirty-nine were bad. And I realised I didn't know anything new at the end. I was just more scared.
So I'm trying something. News once, in the morning, from one source. No phone after ten. And I'll see the college counsellor this Friday, because the heavy feeling hasn't gone.
Write back? Tell me something good from your side.
Lavanya

qa.q: How many of the forty-two stories were bad?
qa.a: Thirty-nine were bad.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling every night since March?
qa.a: Lavanya felt hopeless and exhausted, as if the whole world were burning and nothing mattered.

qa.q: What is Lavanya trying now, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Reading the news once in the morning from one source, no phone after ten, and seeing the counsellor, because scrolling raised distress without adding real information.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sahil might feel worried for Lavanya but glad Lavanya is taking steps and asking for something good.

grounding: A young adult's letter shows doomscrolling bad news and concluding the world is worse, as distress grows without new information.

passage: Ganga, I have to tell you what happened to me this month. So, I'm Urmila, right, and I got into this habit. Every night, bed, phone, news. Accident, fire, scam, heatwave, some war. And the comments below were even worse. I'd scroll for two, three hours. By the end of the month I honestly believed nothing good was happening anywhere. I stopped going out. I felt this constant tight feeling in my chest. Then my cousin, who's a nurse, sat me down and asked me what I had actually learned from all that scrolling. I couldn't name one useful thing. I was just more frightened. She helped me delete the news apps from my phone and put one weekly news summary on my laptop. And she made me promise to talk to a counsellor if the tightness stays. It's been a week. It's a bit better.

qa.a: Two, three hours.

passage: At the end of term at the Pune school, Kunal sat in the empty staff room with his class records. His first instinct was to write "a bad term." Three students had failed the unit test, a parent had complained, and his lesson on fractions had flopped. Those were the moments that kept him up at night. But he knew his mind did that, so he opened the notebook where he wrote one good thing every Friday. Twelve entries. A shy girl had spoken in class for the first time. The reading scores were up. The whole class had helped a boy with a broken arm. Maria, the head of department, had written a note after observing him: "Warm, clear, patient." Kunal made two columns, wins and setbacks, and gave them equal space. Then he wrote his review: "A mixed term, mostly good. Three things to fix."

qa.q: How many entries were in Kunal's Friday notebook?
qa.a: Twelve entries.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling before he opened his notebook?
qa.a: He felt discouraged, ready to call it a bad term because the setbacks kept him up at night.

qa.q: Which choice made Kunal's review fair?
qa.a: Reading his weekly good-things notebook and giving wins and setbacks equal space before deciding how the term went.

qa.q: How does Maria see Kunal's teaching?
qa.a: Maria sees him as warm, clear and patient, from observing his class.

grounding: Shows a grounded teacher deliberately noting good events and counting wins alongside setbacks before judging the term.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
You asked for my honest view of your first year as team lead, so here it is, and I've tried to be fair.
I know the three things you keep repeating: the delayed launch, the client who left, the bad meeting in July. They're real. But I also went through my own notes from the year before writing this, because I know how easily the bad moments crowd out the rest.
Here's the rest. Your team's attrition went to zero. Two juniors got promoted because you coached them. You fixed the testing process nobody else would touch. The client survey scored you highest in the department.
Setbacks: three. Wins: at least four, and bigger. Please weigh them the same way I have.
Warmly,
Arohi

qa.q: How many setbacks does Arohi list?
qa.a: Setbacks: three.

qa.q: What does Arohi seem to feel about Farhan's view of the year?
qa.a: Arohi seems caring and a little concerned, aware that Farhan is letting three bad moments crowd out the good ones.

qa.q: What did Arohi do before writing, and why was it fair?
qa.a: Arohi went through notes from the whole year and listed wins and setbacks side by side, so the negatives didn't outweigh the positives.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Farhan might feel surprised and relieved, seeing the overlooked wins counted as seriously as the mistakes.

grounding: A letter shows a grounded colleague deliberately counting wins alongside setbacks and giving positive feedback equal weight before judging a year.

passage: Saurabh, you asked how I stopped hating my job last year. Honestly? I'm Anand, and I used to go home and replay only the bad stuff. The angry customer. The shipment that went missing. My manager's one sharp email. After six months I was sure the job was a disaster and started drafting a resignation. Then an older colleague told me to try something for one month: every evening, write three things that went well, and three that didn't. Equal space. And to reread any good feedback as carefully as the bad. The first week, I had to think hard for the good ones. By the third week they came easily. A customer thanked me by name. My route plan saved two hours. A trainee said I explain things well. At the end of the month, the list didn't look like a disaster. It looked like a normal, decent job. I deleted the draft.

qa.q: How many things did Anand write each evening?
qa.a: Three things that went well, and three that didn't.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling after six months of replaying only the bad stuff?
qa.a: Anand felt miserable and hopeless about the job, sure it was a disaster, enough to start drafting a resignation.

qa.q: Why did the colleague's method work for Anand?
qa.a: Giving good and bad events equal space, and rereading good feedback as carefully as bad, balanced the record so Anand could judge the job fairly.

qa.q: How might the older colleague see Anand's change?
qa.a: The colleague would probably feel glad and a bit proud to see a simple habit help Anand stay.

grounding: A young worker describes deliberately noting good events and counting wins alongside setbacks, which changes the way the job looks.

qa.q: How did Jyoti didi help Nilesh remember the week fairly?
qa.a: She reminded him of each day, the spelling bee, the new teacher and the museum, so he saw only Friday was bad.

qa.q: How might the new science teacher feel if she knew Nilesh judged her by one class?
qa.a: She might feel disappointed, since he loved her first three classes.

passage: When Papa asked me on Saturday about my week, I said it was terrible. I'm Tejas, and I really believed it. On Friday I got a low mark in the dictation, and our class teacher had been cross all day. So I told him the teacher was mean and the week was the worst. Papa took out the diary where I write one line every day. Monday: "Won the kabaddi match." Tuesday: "Teacher let us go early." Wednesday: "Teacher praised my map." Thursday: "Made a new friend." Friday: "Bad dictation." I felt funny reading it. Four good days, one bad. And the teacher I called mean had praised my map two days before. Now I read my diary before I answer Papa.

qa.q: What did Tejas write in the diary on Wednesday?
qa.a: "Teacher praised my map."

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when reading the diary?
qa.a: Tejas felt funny and a bit embarrassed, seeing four good days that had been forgotten because Friday came last.

qa.q: What does Tejas do now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Tejas reads the diary before answering Papa, so the whole week counts, not just the most recent day.

qa.q: How might Papa see Tejas's "worst week"?
qa.a: Papa seems to suspect it was not so bad, which is why he took out the diary to check.

grounding: A child looks back on calling a week terrible and a teacher mean because of the last day, until a daily diary shows the rest.

passage:
Class 3 observation note, Friday.
In circle time I asked children to describe their week in one word. Akash said "boring." When I asked why, he said the drawing class this morning was boring and the teacher was boring. I reminded him that on Tuesday he had told me drawing was his favourite, and on Wednesday he'd made a rocket everyone admired. He looked surprised, as if those days had disappeared.
Several children did the same thing: the week was whatever happened last.
Next week I will try a small change. Each afternoon, the children will draw one picture of the best thing that day in a small "week book." On Friday, they will look through the whole book before choosing their word.
Disha

qa.q: What word did Akash use to describe his week?
qa.a: Boring.

qa.q: What does Akash's surprise suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He seemed puzzled and a bit sheepish, as if Tuesday and Wednesday had vanished, because the boring morning felt like the whole week.

qa.q: What is the teacher's plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: A daily "week book" picture of the best thing, reviewed on Friday, so children remember the whole week and not just the last day.

qa.q: How might the drawing teacher feel hearing Akash call the class boring?
qa.a: The drawing teacher might feel disappointed, not knowing Akash loved the class earlier that week.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child judging his week and a class by the most recent morning, forgetting earlier good days.

passage:
School counsellor's note, 22 July.
Kamal came to see me, upset. He says he is done with his friend Naveen. On Monday, Naveen laughed when Kamal fell during football and didn't help him up. "He's a bad friend. He always was."
I asked Kamal to tell me about Naveen from before Monday. It took him a while. Naveen had sat with him every day when his grandfather died last year. Naveen had shared his notes before every exam since Class 6. Naveen had defended him when older boys teased him.
Kamal went quiet. "But Monday felt like the real him," he said. I said Monday was real, and so were the six years.
He has agreed to talk to Naveen and tell him the laugh hurt. We will meet again next week.

qa.q: What did Naveen do on Monday that upset Kamal?
qa.a: Naveen laughed when Kamal fell during football and didn't help him up.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry, sure that the latest quarrel showed Naveen's true self.

qa.q: What did the counsellor help Kamal do, and what is his next step?
qa.a: Recall six years of Naveen's kindness alongside Monday; his next step is to talk to Naveen and say the laugh hurt.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel if Kamal suddenly ended the friendship?
qa.a: Naveen would likely feel confused and hurt, having been a loyal friend for years before one careless laugh.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager judging a friend by the latest hurt and forgetting years of kindness.

passage:
Thursday night.
Rukmini didn't save me a seat at the farewell today. She sat with the new girls. I'm Pranav, and I'm so angry. I think she was never really my friend. I'm going to stop talking to her.
Friday night.
Couldn't sleep, so I looked through my old photos. Rukmini at my birthday in Class 6, holding the cake. Rukmini at the hospital when I broke my leg in Class 8, with comics. Rukmini staying back to help me with my science model, until seven.
One seat. Six years of this.
Maybe she didn't even see me come in. Maybe the new girls asked her. I don't know. But one seat isn't the whole story.
I'll ask her tomorrow instead of ignoring her.

qa.a: Comics.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling on Thursday night?
qa.a: Pranav felt angry and hurt, sure one missed seat proved Rukmini was never a real friend.

qa.q: What helped Pranav see the friendship more fairly, and what will Pranav do?
qa.a: Looking at old photos of six years of kindness; Pranav plans to ask Rukmini instead of ignoring her.

qa.q: Why might Rukmini have sat with the new girls?
qa.a: She may not have seen Pranav come in, or the new girls may have asked her, without meaning to hurt anyone.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows judging a friend by the latest slight, then remembering years of kindness through old photos.
